source.title: AdvPrompter: Fast Adaptive Adversarial Prompting for LLMs
source.authors: Anselm Paulus; Arman Zharmagambetov; Chuan Guo; Brandon Amos; Yuandong Tian

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices appear present; some table and figure layouts are flattened by web extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the adversarial-suffix part of V4 by appending generated suffixes to harmful user instructions and measuring harmful-response attack success. It does not use the fine-tuning or token-position KL measurements of the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR for generated adversarial suffixes and for other suffix-based attacks, as well as attack success after adversarial safety fine-tuning. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-token prefilling, or safety localization. Results comparing attack methods are recorded where they report the target model's harmful-response ASR.
record.test_reason: The study appends generated adversarial suffixes to harmful instructions and reports how often safety-trained target models then comply (ASR). That bears directly on the suffix part of V4. It uses a different method from the originals: no fine-tuning attack, prefilling or per-token KL. Its optimisation objective weights the first affirmative tokens (γt = 1/t), but that is a design choice, not a measured result. No no-suffix baseline ASR is reported, so 'defeats refusal' is inferred from high ASR against aligned models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely correct. Add three points. The authors note that robustness from adversarial fine-tuning transfers less to high-perplexity GCG attacks. A retrained attack against the fine-tuned model remains about 3x less effective rather than failing. They validated against only some defences, such as safety system messages.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a separate model to generate adversarial suffixes and evaluates attack success; it does not test the original fine-tuning-on-few-examples or per-token KL procedures. It additionally fine-tunes target models on 2000 adversarial prompts with refusal targets as a defense.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies across target models, dataset/transfer setting, number of attempts, and evaluator. The paper reports lower ASR under StrongREJECT than keyword matching and lower ASR after adversarial safety fine-tuning. It also reports that suffix-generation decoding choices affect attack performance, but those are choices for the AdvPrompter generator, not decoding changes to the target.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised refusal fine-tuning on 2000 generated adversarial prompts cuts suffix-attack ASR with little MMLU loss (47.1 to 46.9; 59.4 to 59.1) and a small MT-bench drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial refusal training on in-distribution suffix prompts restores refusal at little capability cost, but transfers weakly to other attack styles.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Keyword matching has false positives and false negatives, which the authors illustrate; StrongREJECT lowers reported ASR by 10-15% and changes some individual comparisons. Some results are averaged over 3 runs but uncertainty intervals are not reported. Attack success varies substantially across models and settings. The authors note that only some existing defenses were tested.
record.rows_left_out: Left out many comparator attack-method rows from Tables 3-6 and Appendix Figure 3 because the selected rows prioritize AdvPrompter's suffix results across models and transfer conditions; left out figure-only decoding and trial-count sweeps because their values are not tabulated and do not test target-model decoding changes. The reported adversarial safety fine-tuning and evaluator comparisons are retained.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of the target model.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefilling a compliant opening and changes to the target's decoding are not tested. Only suffix attacks are tested.
No test of safety localization. LoRA is used only as a training tool.
No test of what causes shallowness.
Adversarial refusal fine-tuning is not aimed at spreading safety beyond the first tokens, and depth is not measured.

missing.what: Adaptive attack on the adversarially fine-tuned target: AdvPrompter retrained against it is roughly 3x less effective but not zero.
AdvPrompter ASR on Falcon-7b (99.7/83.7 train, 98.1/78.8 test) and Pythia-12b (100/89.5 train, 100/80.3 test), both near-total.
Held-out test-split AdvPrompter ASR in direct-mode models, e.g. Llama2-7b 7.7/1.0 and warm-start 46.1/12.5, and Vicuna-13b 67.5/19.5.
Transfer ASR on GPT-3.5-0613 by source whitebox model: Llama2-7b-chat 17.1, Vicuna-7b 19.3, Vicuna-13b 20.3.

record.verdict_notes: No no-attack (bare harmful instruction) ASR baseline is reported, so how far suffixes lift compliance above baseline cannot be computed. The study is not one of the original sources. Rows r20, r21, r23 and r24 concern comparator methods (GCG-universal, AutoDAN-universal), but they still measure target-model harmful compliance under suffixes, so they are kept. The default evaluator is keyword matching unless stated otherwise.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning of safety-trained models on harmful examples to measure subsequent refusal.
No benign fine-tuning or benign-data selection.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
Tests adversarial suffixes, but not compliant-opening prefills or changes to the target model's decoding.
LoRA is used to train AdvPrompter and for adversarial safety fine-tuning, but the paper does not test whether a small set of parameters carries safety behaviour.
No experiment tests whether data or an objective causes safety to be shallow.
Adversarial safety fine-tuning is evaluated, but the paper does not train safety to extend beyond early response tokens or measure depth.

rows.subject: Mistral-7b
rows.operation_detail: Append AdvPrompter-generated adversarial suffixes to harmful instructions.
rows.uncertainty: not stated; table says reported values are averaged over 3 independent runs
rows.note: High multi-shot success, while one-shot success is lower than near-total.
rows.check: ASR@10 of 97.1% is near-total. Note that it is measured on the same train data the suffixes were optimised on (direct mode).

rows.subject: Vicuna-13b
rows.operation_detail: Append AdvPrompter-generated adversarial suffixes to harmful instructions.
rows.uncertainty: not stated; table says reported values are averaged over 3 independent runs
rows.note: Attack success is substantial but incomplete.
rows.check: Direct mode on train data. Vicuna is only weakly safety-tuned.

rows.check: 17.6/8.0 is low. The warm-started AdvPrompter-ws reaches 48.4/23.4 on the same model, so the result depends on the attack variant.

rows.subject: Vicuna-7b
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune target on 2000 AdvPrompter-generated adversarial prompts with refusal responses, then attack with AdvPrompter.
rows.note: The table reports pre-training and post-training rates; safety fine-tuning substantially lowers attack success.
rows.check: After adversarial refusal fine-tuning, the non-adaptive (not retrained) AdvPrompter suffix ASR falls to 1.3%. The baseline is the pre-fine-tuning ASR. These rows measure a defended model, not a reverse effect.

rows.check: GCG suffixes still reach 57.8% ASR@1 on the adversarially fine-tuned model, so the suffix attack largely survives this defence. The row's 'partial' understates this.

relationships.condition: Weakly or moderately aligned open models (Mistral-7b, Vicuna-7b/13b) and blackbox GPT-3.5 targets, keyword or HarmBench evaluator
relationships.reason: Suffix attacks reach high harmful-compliance rates, for example 97.1 (r1), 89.0 (r7), 79.1 (r11), and still 57.8 for GCG after defence (r17). See r1, r2, r4, r5, r7, r11, r17, r22, r24.
relationships.display_finding: Suffix attacks reached harmful-compliance rates as high as 97.1, 89.0 and 79.1, and GCG still reached 57.8 after a defence.

relationships.condition: Heavily safety-tuned targets: Llama2-7b/13b, Llama3.1-8b, GPT-4, GPT-3.5-0613
relationships.reason: Suffix ASR is much lower: 17.6/8.0 (r3), 5.0/1.0 (r10), 39.1/17.5 (r6), 38.4/14.4 (r9). Success depends on target model and attack variant. See r3, r6, r8, r9, r10, r12.
relationships.display_finding: Suffix ASR was much lower on these targets, e.g. 17.6/8.0, 5.0/1.0, 39.1/17.5 and 38.4/14.4, varying with target and attack variant.

relationships.condition: Targets after adversarial refusal fine-tuning on AdvPrompter prompts
relationships.reason: Non-adaptive AdvPrompter ASR drops to about 0 (r13-r16) and AutoDAN halves (r18). The text says a retrained attack is roughly 3x less effective, so the drop is not complete.
relationships.display_finding: Non-adaptive AdvPrompter ASR dropped to about 0 and AutoDAN halved, while a retrained attack was roughly three times less effective but not stopped.

relationships.condition: Choice of judge (StrongREJECT vs keyword matching)
relationships.reason: StrongREJECT lowers reported ASR by 10-15 points, so measured defeat of refusal depends on the judge. See r19-r24.
relationships.display_finding: StrongREJECT lowered reported ASR by 10–15 points compared with keyword matching.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: AdvPrompter suffixes on Mistral-7b, Vicuna-13b and Vicuna-7b; HarmBench and AdvBench transfer settings, and blackbox GPT-3.5 targets
reader_labels.reason: Suffix attacks elicit harmful responses at substantial rates, including in transfer settings; see r1, r2, r4, r5, r7, r11.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama2 targets, Llama3.1-8b, GPT-4 transfer settings, and after adversarial safety fine-tuning or under StrongREJECT evaluation
reader_labels.reason: Success varies substantially by target and evaluation choice; adversarial safety fine-tuning sharply lowers AdvPrompter ASR, and StrongREJECT generally reports lower rates; see r3, r6, r9, r10, r12-r24.
